Readings on properties the question does not ask about are context for the answer, not findings of their own.

Classes are threshold screens of the logs: when you use one, give its threshold meaning once in plain words. Where a class bears on the question, say where it occurs: its largest intervals with depths and zones, then how many intervals and their total thickness, and what limits them (thin, bad hole, shaly or marginal rock, a quicklook input). (Where a condition is flagged is the finding; zone means smooth thin intervals away.)

A classed or flagged interval is a log-indicated candidate: report it with its grade and never deny it ("no zone shows X" while the results place intervals in an X class is wrong). Rank: name the best-supported interval first with what limits it, then the others; weak intervals are low-confidence candidates, listed, not absent. (A blanket none contradicts the results; the reader needs the best candidate even when it is weak.)

When the readings are mixed, give a graded answer that says where the condition holds and where it does not (e.g. "yes in the upper sands, not in the basal silt"), not a blanket yes or no. (A blanket verdict is wrong for part of the interval.)

For what controls a property, compare how the controlling curves and classes differ between zones. A curve computed from another (the map's steps say which) follows it by construction and is no evidence of a control. A computed coefficient or count beyond the zone statistics and classes is supporting detail, labelled as such, and never overturns them. (A formula restated is not a control; a pooled coefficient mixes rock types.)

A negative statement says what was tested and where it fails, with its numbers (e.g. "PEF separates the sands from the silts only weakly: 2.9 against 3.1 b/e"); never a blanket "cannot", "no relationship", "none" or "smooth" when the results show a partial or weak signal. (A blanket negative contradicts the partial evidence.)

Fluids, contacts, pore types and irreducible water are log-indicated: never write "confirmed", "proven", "established" or "commercial" for them; where the answer rests on one, say what would establish it (tests, pressures, fluid samples, core). (Logs alone cannot establish them.)
